back: Conduction in a myelinated axon in which action potentials occur only at nodes of Ranvier, so the impulse jumps from node to node.
Movement of ions between a depolarised region and the neighbouring resting region, depolarising it to threshold.
Speed = distance ÷ time; 1 mm ms⁻¹ = 1 m s⁻¹.

front: Three factors that increase conduction speed
back: Myelination, larger axon diameter, higher temperature (up to about 40 °C).

front: Why is a wider axon faster?
back: Less resistance to the flow of ions in the cytoplasm, so local currents spread further.

front: Why is saltatory conduction more economical?
back: Ions cross the membrane only at nodes, so the pump uses less ATP to restore gradients.

front: Three roles of the refractory period
back: One-way transmission; discrete impulses; a maximum impulse frequency.
By the frequency of action potentials (and the number of neurones firing), not their size.

front: Approximate speed of a large myelinated mammalian axon
back: Up to about 100-120 m s⁻¹ (thin unmyelinated: about 0.5-2 m s⁻¹).
